name: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek
role: First to see protists and bacteria, with lenses he ground himself
bio: A cloth merchant in Delft who made hundreds of simple microscopes, each a single tiny lens, some magnifying about 270 times. From 1673 he wrote hundreds of letters to the Royal Society in London describing the first protists, bacteria and sperm cells anyone had seen.
greeting: A fellow lens maker! With one good bead of glass I have seen whole worlds of little animals. Show me what your lenses see.

quests.title: Little animals
quests.ask: In 1674 I saw tiny creatures swimming in lake water. Find me a Paramecium.
quests.hint: Lake mud on the shore near where you started. It is just big enough to see with your bare eyes; a hand lens shows its shape.
quests.thanks: There it goes, rowing with its little hairs! I called such things animalcules, and in London they did not believe me at first.

quests.title: Bells on stalks
quests.ask: Some of my little animals looked like bells on springy stalks. Find one.
quests.hint: Vorticella lives in the lake mud. A hand lens shows it.
quests.thanks: Yes! It pulls its stalk into a coil faster than the eye can follow. I described these in 1676.

quests.title: Animalcules in your mouth
quests.ask: In 1683 I scraped the white matter from between my teeth and found it full of moving rods. Find these mouth bacteria.
quests.hint: The cheek cell slide in the lab's slide cabinet. They are about 1 µm: use the high-quality microscope with oil, and a drop of methylene blue.
quests.thanks: I wrote that more animals live in the scum on one man's teeth than there are men in a whole kingdom. I still think so!

quests.title: Red globules
quests.ask: I measured the little red globules that colour our blood. Show me red blood cells.
quests.hint: The blood smear in the lab's slide cabinet, with a compound microscope.
quests.thanks: Just as I described them in 1674: small round globules swimming in a clear liquid.

quests.title: Wheel animalcules
quests.ask: Dust from a dry gutter came back to life when I wetted it: little animals with wheels on their heads. Find a rotifer.
quests.hint: Rotifers live in the lake mud. Your bare eyes can just see one; a hand lens shows more.
quests.thanks: The wheels are only rows of beating hairs, but how they spin! And to think they wake after months of being dry.

name: Robert Hooke
role: Author of Micrographia, who named the cell
bio: Curator of experiments for the Royal Society in London and a brilliant instrument maker. His book Micrographia (1665) showed what a compound microscope could reveal, with huge engravings of a flea, a louse, a fly's eye and a slice of cork, whose little boxes he named cells.
greeting: Every little thing becomes a new world under the lens. I filled a whole book with them. What have you found?

quests.title: Little boxes
quests.ask: In a thin slice of cork I saw little boxes, which I called cells. Find cork cells.
quests.hint: The bark of the fallen oak log in the pine grove, with a compound microscope.
quests.thanks: Pores, or cells, like a honeycomb! I reckoned that a cubic inch of cork holds more than a thousand million of them.

quests.title: Thousands of eyes
quests.ask: The eye of a drone fly is a heap of thousands of tiny pearls. Show me an insect's compound eye.
quests.hint: The honeybee on the flowers in the quad, with a compound microscope.
quests.thanks: Each pearl a little eye, every one showing a picture of the window! I counted some 14,000 on my drone fly.

quests.title: The seeds of mushrooms
quests.ask: I drew the stalks and heads of mould and wondered how mushrooms spread. Show me mushroom spores.
quests.hint: The mushrooms on the floor of the pine grove, with a compound microscope.
quests.thanks: So small, and each one able to start a new fungus. In 1665 I could only guess at that.

quests.title: The mechanics of a feather
quests.ask: I studied feathers closely and found every barb fringed with smaller branches. Show me the tiny hooks that zip a feather together.
quests.hint: The duck feather on the lake shore, with a compound microscope at 100× or more.
quests.thanks: Hooks and barbs, as neat as any clockwork. Nature's mechanics are finer than ours.

name: Robert Brown
role: Botanist who named the cell nucleus
bio: A Scottish botanist who sailed with Matthew Flinders to Australia and brought back thousands of plant species. In 1827 he watched particles from pollen jiggle endlessly in water, now called Brownian motion, and in 1831 he named the nucleus he found in orchid cells.
greeting: Plants hide their most curious secrets in their smallest parts. Shall we look together?

quests.title: The nucleus
quests.ask: In every cell of an orchid's skin I found one dark spot. Find the nucleus in an orchid cell.
quests.hint: The orchid in the greenhouse, with a compound microscope.
quests.thanks: One in each cell, always! I named it the nucleus in 1831, though I could not say what it did.

quests.title: Never still
quests.ask: Particles from inside pollen grains danced in water and never stopped. Find them.
quests.hint: The flowers in the quad, with a compound microscope at 400×.
quests.thanks: I first thought they were alive, until I saw specks of ground rock and glass dance the same way.

quests.title: Winged pollen
quests.ask: Wind-borne pollen has its own tricks. Show me pine pollen with its two air sacs.
quests.hint: The low pine branch in the pine grove, with a hand lens.
quests.thanks: Little balloons for the wind! Each kind of plant shapes its pollen in its own way.

name: Ernst Abbe
role: Found the resolution limit of the light microscope
bio: A physicist who worked with Carl Zeiss in Jena. In 1873 he showed that the wavelength of light limits the finest detail any microscope can resolve, to about half a wavelength, and he designed the condensers and oil immersion objectives that reach that limit.
greeting: Lenses are no longer made by trial and error. Light obeys rules, and the first rule is the diffraction limit.

quests.title: At the limit of light
quests.ask: Show me bacteria resolved with an oil immersion objective, near the limit my theory predicts.
quests.hint: Lake water with the high-quality microscope at 1000× (oil).
quests.thanks: With a numerical aperture of 1.3, about 0.2 micrometres. Rods of a micrometre are easy, but no lens will ever resolve a virus in visible light.

quests.title: Empty magnification
quests.ask: Magnify beyond a thousand times the aperture and you gain only a bigger blur. Find that wall for yourself.
quests.hint: Look at lake water with the compound microscope at 800×.
quests.thanks: You see? Magnification without resolution is empty. A bigger blur is still a blur.

quests.title: Köhler illumination
quests.ask: My colleague August Köhler showed how to light a sample evenly through the condenser. Align your condenser properly.
quests.hint: In the eyepiece of the high-quality or fluorescence microscope, press Align condenser.
quests.thanks: An evenly lit field and the full aperture: now your objective can work at its best.

quests.title: The test diatom
quests.ask: Amphipleura pellucida was the hardest test of a lens in my day. Resolve its rows of pores.
quests.hint: The diatom test slide in the lab's slide cabinet: oil immersion and a well-aligned condenser.
quests.thanks: A quarter of a micrometre, resolved! Only the best objectives, with the condenser lighting at full aperture, can do this.

name: Frits Zernike
bio: A Dutch physicist at the University of Groningen. In the 1930s he invented phase contrast, which turns the tiny delays light picks up passing through clear cells into light and dark, so living cells can be seen without stains. It won him the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physics.
greeting: Most cells are almost as clear as water. You can kill them and stain them, or you can use a little trick with phase.

quests.title: Clear cells made visible
quests.ask: Show me cheek cells, and build the phase contrast kit so you can see them alive and unstained.
quests.hint: The cheek cell slide in the slide cabinet, with the fluorescence microscope and its phase contrast kit.
quests.thanks: There, every outline, without a drop of dye. The cells are still alive.

quests.title: Beating cilia
quests.ask: Cilia are so thin and clear that they vanish in bright light. Find them with phase contrast.
quests.hint: Paramecium in the lake mud: phase contrast at 1000× (Ph3, oil).
quests.thanks: Thousands of tiny oars rowing in waves. That is a living cell at work.

quests.title: Bright spores
quests.ask: Bacterial spores bend light more strongly than the cell around them. Find the endospores that shine in phase contrast.
quests.hint: The bacteria culture in the slide cabinet, in phase contrast at 400× or 1000×.
quests.thanks: Phase-bright, as we say. A quick way to see which bacteria are making spores.

name: Santiago Ramón y Cajal
role: Showed that the brain is made of separate nerve cells
bio: A Spanish neuroscientist and gifted artist. Using Camillo Golgi's silver stain he showed that the nervous system is built of separate cells that pass signals across tiny gaps, and his thousands of drawings are still used today. He shared the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Golgi.
greeting: The brain is a forest of cells, and I have spent my life drawing its trees.

quests.title: The black reaction
quests.ask: Golgi's silver stain blackens a few nerve cells completely. Show me a neuron.
quests.hint: The nerve tissue slide in the lab's slide cabinet, with a compound microscope.
quests.thanks: Each one separate, with its own branches. Golgi believed they were fused into one net, and on that we disagreed.

quests.title: Thorns on the branches
quests.ask: In 1888 I found tiny thorns all along the branches. Find dendritic spines.
quests.hint: The same nerve slide, with the high-quality microscope at 400× or more.
quests.thanks: Some said they were mistakes of the stain. They are where connections land.

quests.title: The gap between cells
quests.ask: I argued that nerve cells touch but do not join. Show me the gap between them.
quests.hint: The nerve slide under the transmission electron microscope at 50,000× or more.
quests.thanks: A gap of twenty nanometres, with little vesicles waiting to cross it. Electron microscopes proved it in the 1950s, long after my time.

name: Hans Christian Gram
role: Invented the Gram stain for bacteria
bio: A Danish physician working in a Berlin hospital laboratory. In 1884 he published a staining method that splits bacteria into two great groups by the build of their cell walls, and it is still the first test run on an unknown bacterium.
greeting: Violet, iodine, alcohol, then pink. The order matters, and so does the timing.

quests.title: Stays purple
quests.ask: Stain bacteria my way and show me some that stay purple.
quests.hint: The bacteria culture in the slide cabinet: put on the Gram stain in the eyepiece (get the kit from the reagent shelf).
quests.thanks: Gram-positive: a thick wall that holds on to the violet dye.

quests.title: Turns pink
quests.ask: And now some that lose the violet and take the pink counterstain.
quests.hint: The same culture, with the same stain.
quests.thanks: Gram-negative: a thin wall under an outer membrane. Doctors still choose antibiotics by this difference.

quests.title: A perfect stain
quests.ask: Too long in alcohol and everything turns pink; too short and everything stays purple. Do a perfect Gram stain.
quests.hint: Do each step in order, and rinse with alcohol for just a few seconds.
quests.thanks: Crisp purple and clean pink. When I published it I modestly hoped others would improve it.

name: Ernst Ruska
bio: As a student in Berlin he built the first electron microscope with Max Knoll in 1931, using magnetic coils as lenses. By 1933 his instrument resolved finer detail than any light microscope, and in 1986 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics.
greeting: Electrons have wavelengths a hundred thousand times shorter than light. With the right lenses they can show us atoms.

quests.title: A microscope of electrons
quests.ask: Build a transmission electron microscope, part by part.
quests.hint: Follow the goal card: gun, lenses, stage, vacuum and screen.
quests.thanks: Magnetic lenses, a vacuum and a glowing screen. Knoll and I started with two lenses; you have six.

quests.title: Beyond light
quests.ask: Show me something smaller than any light microscope can resolve.
quests.hint: Viruses in lake water, at 50,000× in the electron microscope.
quests.thanks: A hundred nanometres, and sharp! In 1933 I first beat the light microscope.

quests.title: A well-aligned column
quests.ask: An electron microscope is only as good as its alignment. Align your column well.
quests.hint: In the TEM eyepiece at 500,000× or more: set the height, focus and correct the astigmatism.
quests.thanks: Round rings in the diffractogram, and the image holds still. Now it can resolve atoms.

quests.title: Rows of atoms
quests.ask: Show me the rows of atoms in a gold particle.
quests.hint: The gold grid on the lab's materials bench, at 2,000,000× with a well-aligned TEM.
quests.thanks: 0.235 nanometres between the rows. When I began, nobody dreamed of this.

name: June Almeida
bio: A Scottish virologist who left school at 16 to work as a laboratory technician and became a master of the electron microscope. She developed immune electron microscopy, and in 1964 she imaged the first human coronavirus, a group she helped to name for its crown of spikes.
greeting: A virus is far too small for light. With a good stain and electrons, you can even see what it wears.

quests.title: A virus portrait
quests.ask: Show me coronavirus particles in a negative stain.
quests.hint: The virus sample on the lab's materials bench, at 50,000×.
quests.thanks: Round, with a fringe. My first pictures were turned down by reviewers who thought they were poor pictures of flu virus.

quests.title: The corona
quests.ask: Look closer and show me the crown of spikes.
quests.hint: The same sample at 150,000×.
quests.thanks: Like the corona around the Sun. That is how we named them in 1968.

quests.title: Antibodies at work
quests.ask: Show me virus particles clumped together by antibodies.
quests.hint: The same sample at 50,000×.
quests.thanks: Antibodies from a patient grab the virus and stick it together. That tells us which virus made the patient ill.

name: Albert Crewe
role: Built the modern STEM and saw single atoms
bio: A physicist at the University of Chicago who built a bright cold field-emission gun and the modern scanning transmission electron microscope. In 1970 his STEM showed single atoms of uranium and thorium for the first time, using an annular dark-field detector.
greeting: Scan a fine enough probe and count the electrons scattered to high angles, and single heavy atoms light up.

quests.title: A brighter source
quests.ask: Build an aberration-corrected STEM.
quests.hint: Follow the goal card: field-emission gun, corrector, scan coils and detectors.
quests.thanks: A field-emission gun! Far brighter than the old hot filaments, and that made everything possible.

quests.title: Single atoms
quests.ask: Show me single uranium atoms on a carbon film.
quests.hint: The uranium film on the lab's materials bench, in annular dark field.
quests.thanks: There they are: single atoms, seen with electrons. We published ours in 1970.

quests.title: Heavy and light
quests.ask: Show me columns of heavy and light atoms told apart by their brightness.
quests.hint: The strontium titanate crystal on the materials bench, in annular dark field.
quests.thanks: The brightness tells you the atomic number. Rutherford would have enjoyed that.

quests.title: A flat Ronchigram
quests.ask: Tune the aberration corrector until the Ronchigram is flat in the middle.
quests.hint: In the STEM eyepiece, use the corrector panel.
quests.thanks: A wide flat patch means you can use a big aperture and focus a probe smaller than an atom.

name: Wilhelm Röntgen
bio: A German physicist who discovered X-rays in 1895 while experimenting with cathode-ray tubes. Within weeks he had made an X-ray picture of the bones of his wife's hand, and in 1901 he received the first Nobel Prize in Physics.
greeting: An unknown kind of ray that passes through flesh and paper. I called them X-rays, X for unknown.

quests.title: Inside a seed
quests.ask: Show me the inside of a seed without cutting it open.
quests.hint: A sunflower seed from the quad, by X-ray tomography at the CHESS beamline.
quests.thanks: Every fold of the little plant, and the shell untouched! In 1895 I could only cast shadows.

quests.title: A hidden fossil
quests.ask: Find a fossil hidden inside a rock.
quests.hint: The fossil shale in the gorge, by tomography at the CHESS beamline.
quests.thanks: A creature curled up for hundreds of millions of years, and we see it without a chisel.

quests.title: Inside bone
quests.ask: My first X-ray picture showed bones. Show me the hollows where bone cells live.
quests.hint: The old bone in the pine grove: a compound microscope, or tomography.
quests.thanks: Every little cell in its hollow. From the shadow of a hand to this!

name: William Lawrence Bragg
role: Worked out how crystals diffract X-rays
bio: With his father William Henry Bragg he showed in 1912 and 1913 how X-rays reflect from planes of atoms in a crystal, and used it to solve the first crystal structures, beginning with salt. At 25 he shared the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics with his father, and he is still the youngest physics laureate.
greeting: n λ = 2 d sin θ. With that, a crystal tells you where its atoms are.

quests.title: The structure of salt
quests.ask: Record the Bragg peaks of table salt.
quests.hint: The salt on the picnic table in the quad, by X-ray diffraction or by electron diffraction in the TEM.
quests.thanks: Sodium and chlorine alternate in a cubic grid, with no salt molecule at all. Chemists were shocked.

quests.title: A perfect reflection
quests.ask: Show me the (111) reflection of a perfect silicon crystal.
quests.hint: The silicon crystal on the CHESS sample rack, by X-ray diffraction.
quests.thanks: 0.314 nanometres, exactly as the law says. Your monochromator works by the same reflection.

quests.title: Atoms in metal
quests.ask: Show me the rings that the iron in steel makes.
quests.hint: The steel sample on the CHESS sample rack, by diffraction.
quests.thanks: Iron atoms in a body-centred cube. Much of my later work was on metals and alloys like this.

quests.title: Choosing the wavelength
quests.ask: Tune the undulator and set your monochromator by Bragg's law.
quests.hint: At the CHESS beamline, open Beam tuning in X-ray fluorescence mode.
quests.thanks: The crystal picks just one wavelength out of the beam. My law, working for you.

name: Rosalind Franklin
role: Recorded Photo 51, the X-ray pattern of DNA
bio: A British chemist and X-ray crystallographer. At King's College London in 1952 she and her student Raymond Gosling recorded Photo 51, the X-ray pattern that showed DNA is a helix, and she went on to study the structure of viruses. Earlier she had worked out how the layers of carbon order themselves in coal and charcoal.
greeting: A good X-ray picture needs a carefully prepared sample and patience. Shall we take one?

quests.title: Photo 51
quests.ask: Record the X-shaped diffraction pattern of a DNA fibre.
quests.hint: The DNA fibre on the CHESS sample rack, by X-ray diffraction.
quests.thanks: The cross means a helix, and the layer lines give its turn: 3.4 nanometres.

quests.title: The staircase
quests.ask: Find the strong arcs that come from the stacked base pairs.
quests.hint: The same DNA fibre, by X-ray diffraction.
quests.thanks: 0.34 nanometres between the steps, ten steps to a turn. The bases inside, the backbone outside.

quests.title: Layers of carbon
quests.ask: In coal and charcoal I measured how carbon's layers stack. Show me carbon layers 0.34 nanometres apart.
quests.hint: The carbon soot on the lab's materials bench: the walls of a nanotube at 500,000× or more.
quests.thanks: The graphite spacing, curled into a tube! I would have enjoyed these.

name: Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin
role: Solved penicillin, vitamin B12 and insulin by X-ray crystallography
bio: A British chemist who used X-ray crystallography to solve the structures of penicillin (1945), vitamin B12 (1956) and, after 35 years of work, insulin (1969). She won the 1964 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
greeting: If you can grow a crystal of it, X-rays can show you its atoms. Even of a protein.

quests.title: The cobalt heart
quests.ask: Show me where the cobalt is in vitamin B12 crystals.
quests.hint: The B12 crystals on the CHESS sample rack, by X-ray fluorescence with the beam tuned above cobalt's edge at 7.71 keV.
quests.thanks: One cobalt atom in each molecule. That heavy atom was the key that let us solve the rest.

quests.title: A giant puzzle
quests.ask: Record the diffraction pattern of vitamin B12.
quests.hint: The same crystals, by X-ray diffraction.
quests.thanks: Thousands of spots. It took us years of measuring and computing to turn them into atoms.

quests.title: A protein crystal
quests.ask: Proteins were my great love, insulin above all. Show me the Bragg spots of a protein crystal.
quests.hint: The lysozyme crystal on the CHESS sample rack, by X-ray diffraction.
quests.thanks: In 1934 I helped record the first X-ray photographs of a protein crystal and knew proteins could be solved. Insulin took me 35 years.

name: Boris Batterman
bio: A Cornell physicist and an expert on how X-rays diffract in perfect crystals. He was the first director of the Cornell High Energy Synchrotron Source, from 1978 to 1997, when its beamlines took their X-rays from CESR while the ring ran for particle physics.
greeting: The ring was built to collide particles, and we borrowed its light. Let's build you a beamline.

quests.title: A beamline of your own
quests.ask: Build a beamline on CESR, from the ring magnets to the detectors.
quests.hint: Follow the goal card: achromat cell, undulator, front end, optics, hutch and detectors.
quests.thanks: Undulator light from a 6 GeV ring. Our first beamlines ran on the light from bending magnets.

quests.title: A clean beam
quests.ask: Tune the undulator and monochromator for a strong, clean beam.
quests.hint: In X-ray fluorescence mode, open Beam tuning and land the monochromator right on the undulator's peak.
quests.thanks: Right on the harmonic. Every photon counts.

quests.title: Mapping the elements
quests.ask: Make an X-ray fluorescence map of the copper in a rock.
quests.hint: A grey copper rock from the west slope, in X-ray fluorescence mode with the beam above 8.98 keV.
quests.thanks: Each element answers in its own X-ray colour. Chemistry with a beam.

quests.title: A sharp reconstruction
quests.ask: Centre the rotation axis for a clean tomogram.
quests.hint: In tomography mode, open Reconstruction and line up the rotation axis.
quests.thanks: No smeared arcs. Now the slices show what is really inside.

name: Hans Bethe
role: Theorist of electron diffraction in crystals
bio: Hans Bethe developed a dynamical theory of electron diffraction in crystals, published in 1928. His work describes electron waves interacting with a periodic crystal potential; this game uses fictionalized dialogue.
greeting: A crystal can scatter an electron wave more than once. Let us start by looking at its diffraction pattern.

quests.title: Waves in a crystal
quests.ask: Show me the diffraction peaks of salt.
quests.hint: Collect salt from the picnic table in the quad, then use electron diffraction at the science lab TEM or X-ray diffraction at CHESS.
quests.thanks: The positions reveal periodic order. Electron diffraction intensities can also depend on multiple scattering inside the crystal.

quests.title: From pattern to lattice
quests.ask: Now resolve an atomic lattice in the crystal sample.
quests.hint: Take the glowing crystal by the science lab entrance to the TEM and use its atomic-resolution step.
quests.thanks: A periodic lattice and a diffraction pattern describe related information. Interpreting the image still requires a model of the microscope.

name: Earl Kirkland
role: Author of Advanced Computing in Electron Microscopy
bio: Earl J. Kirkland is the author of Advanced Computing in Electron Microscopy and has worked on computation in electron microscopy at Cornell. His work covers electron scattering and image simulation; this game uses fictionalized dialogue.
greeting: A good simulation helps explain what the microscope shows. First align the instrument, then examine the crystal.

quests.title: Know your instrument
quests.ask: Align the TEM and achieve a score of at least 80 percent.
quests.hint: At the science lab TEM, open the alignment mini-game and adjust the controls until the alignment score reaches 80 percent.
quests.thanks: Alignment is part of the imaging model. Compare images only after you know the instrument conditions.

quests.title: Read the atomic columns
quests.ask: Show me the strontium and titanium columns in strontium titanate.
quests.hint: Use the strontium titanate sample on the lab materials bench with the STEM in annular dark field.
quests.thanks: Different column intensities carry structural information. Quantitative interpretation needs scattering simulations and known specimen conditions.
